People under it hold conversations with the dead and do not know the dead are dead. They pick at threads that are not there. They lose days and believe they lost a night. It is the one door a person can walk through and back and never once know they left.

It is also, plainly, dangerous. The same compounds race the heart, stop the breath, and drive the body’s temperature up to killing heights, and they can do all of this even in small amounts — the gap between the dose that opens the door and the dose that stops the heart is cruelly narrow, and nobody can measure it from the inside. The eyes blow wide and the skin goes hot and dry and the mouth goes to paper; a kind of blindness can set in that lasts for days. Children who find the spiny seed-pods and eat the seeds have died of it, quickly and terribly.

And there is a longer, slower cost, which this book leans on and which should be named honestly. Years of blocking that same brain-signal appear to wear the mind down. The best evidence we have is not about this plant but about ordinary medicines that work the same way — a large study followed older people for years and found that the more of these acetylcholine-blocking drugs a person took, over time, the more likely they were to slip into lasting forgetting. It is a fair inference, not a proven chain, that fifty years at this particular door would take its toll the same way — that the forgetting is the fare. This book treats it as the fare. The reader should know that the inference is the author’s, drawn across a gap in what is actually known.

Nothing in these pages happens that the flower cannot do. Where the book shows a woman kept company, nightly, for fifty years, by someone who is gone, it is not reaching for a metaphor. That is, exactly and clinically, the kind of thing this plant does to the people who go to it. The only liberty taken is to believe that it mattered to her — and that, the flower has nothing to say about either way.
THE MAPMAKER
The people who charted this particular door did not go looking for a drug. They went looking for a vanishing language, and the door came with it.

Most of what is known about momoy — the sacred datura of the Santa Barbara coast — survives because of one obsessive man. John Peabody Harrington was a linguist who spent the first decades of the twentieth century, roughly 1912 to 1928, among the last fluent Chumash speakers, writing down everything they would tell him: words, place-names, recipes, and the old stories, faster than the language was dying. He published almost none of it. He left behind an enormous disordered mass of field notes that scholars are still working through a century later.

It was from that mass that the anthropologist Thomas Blackburn drew the collection December’s Child: A Book of Chumash Oral Narratives (University of California Press, 1975), and it is there that momoy appears not as a plant but as a person. In the stories she is an old woman, a widow, living alone at the edge of the world, who could see a little way into the future; who did not die in the Flood but became the datura; and who shows those who drink of her their own fate — the parts still coming, and the parts already lost. The old tellings hold that a living person who could look at his own soul this way need not fear death. They also hold, without flinching, that not everyone who drank came back.

For the wider story of the plant — how far it reaches, how many peoples found their way to it independently, from the valley of Mexico to the Virginia tidewater — the standard account is the lifework of the Harvard botanist Richard Evans Schultes, who spent his career mapping the plants that open doors and set datura among the oldest and most widespread of them.

And then there is the plant’s other, harder name. In 1676, in the wreckage of Bacon’s Rebellion, soldiers sent to the Virginia colony boiled the local weed for a meal and spent eleven days out of their minds and happy, remembering nothing after. The colonist

Robert Beverley set the story down in his History and Present State of Virginia in 1705, and the place where it happened gave the plant the name most of the English-speaking world still uses for it. The Chumash had a gentler name, and an older one, and theirs is the one on the map at the front of this book.
